birdSongJournal.description: Asks BirdWeather which birds its listening stations actually heard near you. Every new species gets a field-journal plate drawn by OpenAI from BirdWeather's licensed reference photo, verified for accuracy, and saved to the asset collection. Cycles through the collection on each render.

fields.hint: Centre of the listening area. Leave this and the station IDs empty to pause the journal.
fields.label: Latitude
fields.name: latitude

fields.hint: BirdWeather stations are sparse outside cities — widen this if nothing turns up.
fields.label: Radius (km)
fields.name: radiusKm

fields.hint: Comma-separated. Set this to follow specific stations (your own PUC, say) and the area above is ignored.
fields.label: BirdWeather station IDs
fields.name: stationIds

fields.hint: Only birds heard within this many days count.
fields.label: Time window (days)
fields.name: daysWindow

fields.hint: How often to ask BirdWeather what it has been hearing.
fields.label: Poll every (minutes)

fields.hint: How many of the most-heard species to take from each poll
fields.label: Species per poll

fields.hint: Ignore species heard fewer times than this in the window — BirdNET's one-off guesses
fields.label: Minimum detections

fields.label: Classifications

fields.label: Plate style
fields.name: style
fields.value: A 19th-century naturalist's field-journal plate on lightly aged cream paper: fine ink linework with soft watercolor washes. The bird perches on a small branch or stands in typical habitat, anatomically accurate, with its bill open mid-song. Around it, small pencil detail studies (head, wing or feather), a small hand-drawn sonogram or sound-wave sketch in one margin as if the bird had been logged by ear, and short handwritten-style margin notes. Neatly hand-lettered at the bottom: the common name in larger letters and the scientific name in italics beneath it.
